title: How to Use Docker in this Class
text:
What is Docker?
Docker is a collection of technologies that allow developers to run applications in isolated environments. For example, a company like Netflix might use multiple containers to isolate different parts of the user experience (logging in to your account, billing, selecting a series to binge). In the realm of data analysis, researchers and analysts use Docker to package fragile software stacks, such as a specific version of Julia, Python, or R combined with custom libraries and GPU drivers, so that data processing, modeling, and other pipelines can be shared and run anywhere without breaking. In either setting, careful management of the computing environments under which discrete tasks are carried out is a central concern.

title: How to Use Docker in this Class
text:
Why are we using Docker?
While there are many ways in which containers might be applied, our interest in isolated environments is motivated by the following:

Standarization and Consistency. Everyone in the class will run the same OS, the same system dependencies, and identical software versions.
Minimal Installation Friction. There is a benefit to learning how to manage systems on your own, from scratch, as you build out your workspace and tools. Unfortunately, the quarter system does not allow much time for exploration, experimentation, and failure. Most of the hard work has been handled by building the class Docker image.
Reproducbility. Containerization helps us practice reproducbility in our work. It makes for good science, good software, and excellent communication of your work.

title: How to Use Docker in this Class
section: So how do I use it?
text:
So how do I use it?
There are few terms we need to define before we use Docker.

Dockerfile: This is a recipe that defines an environment. It’s just a text file with Bash commands (usually) and some additional Docker-specific syntax.
Image: This is the product generated by running the recipe in a Dockerfile. It is a read-only environment, configured with a specific Operating System (OS), file structure, and accompanying software.
Container: Whereas images are static, containers are dynamic. It is the “runtime” or how we use a Docker image. A single image can be used to spin up multiple containers, each running instances of the same or related applications. The environment is the same each time you create a container, from scratch, using the same image.
Volume: You can create and destroy data within a container, but Docker containers are deliberately disposable. A (storage) volume allows you to persist data after you shut down a container. This works by mapping data (files, folders, programs, etc) from a container to your disk.
Docker Desktop: The main software from Docker that we will use, which handles building images, container creation, and deployment.


1. Download and Install Docker Desktop
Point your preferred web browser to https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/ and select the appropriate download for your OS and architecture.






WarningWindows Users




If you have a Surface or Copilot+ laptop, it has a Qualcomm Snapdragon CPU. Select the ARM64 option.
Otherwise, you have an Intel or AMD CPU. Select the AMD64 option.



Follow instructions from the installer.


2. Download our docker-compose.yml

This is a file to automatically construct a container from pre-built images.
Please download it from Canvas.
Be sure to download it to a convenient location where you would like to store your course materials.







WarningWindows Users



Avoid placing your course materials, including docker-compose.yml, inside a folder that is backed up by cloud services like OneDrive or Google Drive. The automated nature of such tools risk corrupting your files if a backup triggers while your container is running, resulting in data loss.
Suggested Workaround: Store your work directly under your C:\ drive; for example C:\STAT206.




3. Create your local container
First, open the terminal view in Docker Desktop.





Next, navigate to the folder/directory containing the docker-compose.yml file. Once you’ve verified the file’s presence, enter and run the command docker compose up -d msba.





The Containers tab in Docker Desktop shows the status of your container.






Gray circle: Not running
Green circle: Running (in the background)
You can start/stop the container using the Play/Stop button under Actions.

The docker ps command can also be used to monitor your container from a CLI.







4. Using the Container
If you want to access the container from your machine’s Terminal:
docker start -ai STAT206-MSBA

docker start: The start action will only start an existing container.
-ai: The option a ensures we can see messages in our terminal and propagates signals (such as force quitting). The option i is used to indicate an interactive session.
STAT206-MSBA the name of the container we wish to run.

If you just want the container to run in the background so you can connect to it using VSCode:
docker start STAT206-MSBA
You can stop a running container using:
docker stop STAT206-MSBA

title: Configure Git
text:
Overview
We will use Git for version control of our work throughout the quarter. You will spend most of your time working in a single-user setting, editing and managing your own repository for assignments. Later in the course you will work in a small team and use Git to coordinate development.
Before that can happen, we’ll need to configure Git.






NoteConfiguration Files



Dr. Landeros prefers to use a ~/.config/ directory to store configuration files as much as possible. This practice is based on the XDG Base Directory Specification, which a tool like Git respects. That said, not every tool across Linux distributions will adhere to this standard.

title: Configure Git
text:
Method 1: Quick and easy
The following commands will create a global configuration file at ~/.gitconfig.
git config --global user.name "CHOSE YOUR NAME"
git config --global user.email "UCR EMAIL"
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

title: Configure Git
text:
Method 2: Using an editor

Create and open a file: ~/.config/git/config. Alternatively, you may use a file at ~/.gitconfig. Just choose whichever approach appeals to you.
In the file, type in the following information (mind the indentation):
[user]
    name = CHOOSE YOUR NAME
    email = UCR EMAIL
[core]
    editor = code --wait

title: Configure Git
section: What does the core.editor option do?
text:
What does the core.editor option do?
If you run git commit in a Git repository, the command set for core.editor is run automatically for you. This is convenient for quickly drafting a commit message.
Alternatively, you can use the VSCode interface for writing commits.

title: Configure Git
text:
Check your work

Read the contents of ~/.config/git/config
Check the output of git config --global --list.
Check the output of git config --global --list --show-source.

title: Configure Git
text:
Optional: Address colorblindness
By default, the command git diff relies on red (for deletions) and green (for additions) to highlight changes in files. Other Git commands use red and green to tag the state of varies files in a repository. Fortunately, the tool can be configured to use colorblind-friendly alternatives and increase its accessibility.

Option 1: Change the diff colors
In a command line:
git config --global color.diff.old "yellow"
git config --global color.diff.new "blue"
Alternatively, edit your Git configuration file:
[color "diff"]
    old = yellow
    new = blue


Option 2: Disable color-coded output
In a command line:
git config --global color.ui false
Alternatively, edit your Git configuration file:
[color]
    ui = false

title: Control Flow
text:
Overview
Literals, variables, and built-in/package functions are quite useful but insufficient for writing complex scripts and programs. Here we briefly review syntax for conditional statements and repeated evaluation. These two concepts vastly increase the expressiveness of any programming language. We then shift our attention to user-defined functions, highlighting scoping rules and other features in Julia.

title: Control Flow
text:
Conditional Statements
Conditional statements allow a program to change its behavior based on some state, usually captured by one or more variables.

if condition1
  # do something
elseif condition2
  # do something
else
  # do something
end

Here, condition1 and condition2 must be Julia expressions that evaluate to true or false. There are a few points to be aware of:

Most programming languages treat true and false as 1 and 0 (integers). This is true in Julia, but the reverse is not allowed.
Julia uses the Missing type to represent missingness, and Nothing to represent void. The former can appear as the result of a Boolean expression. The proper way to check for missingness or nothingness is to use ismissing() or isnothing(), respectively.
Conditional statements can be chained and nested.
Whitespace does not have special meaning in Julia. Thus, it is perfectly acceptable to write
The order in which you check conditions matters!


if condition something end







Important



Every conditional statement introduces a branch in your code. Excessive branching may obscure intended meaning and potentially slow down your code.



Example: Checking for an empty collection

mydata = Int[] # array of Ints
if isempty(mydata)
  push!(mydata, 100)
else
  mydata[1] = 100
end

The cell above displays an array with 1 element.

Which branch was executed?
Why do we see any return value at all?



Example: A biased coin flip

u = rand()
if u < 1/3
  println("Heads")
else
  println("Tails")
end

The code above behaves randomly because the printed message depends on the value of u.

What is the probability of seeing the outcome "Tails"?
Justify your answer to the question above.
What about the probability of seeing "heads"?



Shorthand: Elvis Operator
Like other languages, Julia supports the “ternary” operator ?:, sometimes referred to as the Elvis operator. It is shorthand for if-else, but it can be chained to mimic if-elseif-else (don’t do that!).

condition1 ? alternativeA : alternativeB



Example: Writing a quick message

mymood = abs(randn()) > 1.96 ? "jubilant" : "downtrodden"
explanation = mymood == "jubilant" ? "" : "failed to"
println("Just so you know, so-and-so is absolutely $(mymood) because their simulation $(explanation) converged.")


Explain why there is an extra space whenever so-and-so’s mood is jubilant.



Functional Version: ifelse()
The performance of code with hot loops (that is, code that is expected to execute thousands of times in a program or script) can be quite sensitive to minor tweaks. One example is the presence of branches. Modern CPUs are equipped with aggressive branch predictors that attempt to mitigate the cost of branching but they have limitations.
In some cases, it may be cheaper to avoid branching altogether by paying the cost of executing both branches. This is precisely the purpose of ifelse() in the Julia language:

x = 0.5 * randn()

# this branches (maybe)
if x < 0
  x^2
else
  sqrt(x)
end


# this does not branch
# both expressions below are evaluated before checking the condition.
ifelse(x < 0, x^2, sqrt(x))


ifelse(true, 0, error("stop execution!"))







Noteifelse() in other languages



In the Python and R languages, the ifelse() function is primarily used to vectorize conditional statements. Julia’s version also supports vectorization, e.g. ifelse.(condition, x, y).

title: Control Flow
text:
Repeated Evaluation

for Loop

for i in 1:10
  println(i)
end

Just like condtional statements, loops can be nested.

for i in 1:10
  for j in 1:5
    println(i * j)
  end
end

Julia supports nesting within a single line:

for i in 1:10, j in 1:5
  println(i * j)
end



while Loop

while condition1
  # do something
end



Loop Overrides
You can break out of innermost loop.

for i in 1:10
  # do something
  if condition1
    break # skip remaining loop
  end
end

You can also continue to skip over a particular iteration.

for i in 1:10
  # do something
  if condition1
    continue # skip to next iteration
  end
  # do something
end



Example: Displaying a Tic-Tac-Toe board
A Tic-Tac-Toe board consists of 9 spaces arranged in a 3 by 3 grid. If we include characters to represent the grid, then we need 5 characters per row for a total of 25 characters. Let’s display an empty board:

for i in 1:5
  row_i = ""
  if iszero(i % 2)
    row_i *= "─┼─┼─"
  else
    for j in 1:5
      row_i *= ifelse(iszero(j % 2), "│", " ")
    end
  end
  println(row_i)
end



Compatibility with Iterators
Loops in Julia are compatible with any iterable object. For example, the built-in collections in Julia implement the iteration interface.

x = [10, 20, 30]

for item in x
  println(item)
end


for (i, item) in enumerate(x)
  println("index: ", i, ", value: ", item)
end


for item in reverse(x)
  println(item)
end


d = Dict("Alice" => 4, "Bob" => 2)
for (key, val) in d
  println("They key $(key) maps to value $(val)")
end







TipLaziness is a virtue



The reverse() function above does not sort() the array x! Instead, it exploits the structure of the underlying data type to reverse the iteration. This avoids memory allocation and extra computation.








TipIteration Style



The proper style for iterating over an Array is to use eachindex() or axes(). The reason is that, while Julia uses 1-based indexing, it supports arbitrary indexing styles.

title: Control Flow
text:
Error Handling
Julia provides several built-in exception types to handle errors or otherwise halt execution and display an informative message.

1 / 0     # division expanding to floating point
div(1, 0) # Euclidean division (integers only)


error("Eternity lies ahead of us, and behind. Have you drunk your fill?")

In many cases, it is enough to use an assertion with @assert.

x = -1
@assert x >= 0
sqrt(x)

title: Introduction to Algorithms
text:
Let’s consider a few computational tasks which can be implemented with different algorithms.

Dictionary definition: A set of instructions for doing something; input to output.
Donald Knuth’s definition in The Art of Computer Programming, Chapter 1: (1) Finiteness, (2) Definiteness, (3) Input, (4) Output, and (5) Effectiveness.

The examples here happen to be positive examples of recursion, though their implementation on a computer may not use recursion.


Given data \(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}\) as \(n\) real numbers, the sample mean and variance are
\[\begin{align*}
\mu_{n}
&= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} \\
s_{n}^{2}
&= \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \mu_{n})^{2}.
\end{align*}\]
We seek a method to update the sample estimates after receiving a new observation, \(x_{n+1}\). This presents a few issues:

If \(n\) is large (say \(\ge 10^{9}\)), then recomputing the estimates from scratch is wasteful.
Alternatively, we may be operating in a streaming setting in which we anticipate receiving many more additional observations in the future at unknown times.

With a bit of algebra, one can easily rewrite these formulas in a recursive form. For the sample mean we have
\[\begin{align*}
\mu_{n+1}
&=
\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} x_{i} \\
&=
\frac{1}{n+1} \times \frac{n}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} + \frac{1}{n+1} x_{n+1} \\
&=
\frac{n}{n+1} \mu_{n} + \frac{1}{n+1} x_{n+1}.
\end{align*}\]
Given the current estimate \(\mu_{n}\), we can update the sample mean with the new observation \(x_{n+1}\). The key feature of this algorithm is that it is a one-pass procedure in which we use each data point once and only once. There are similar formulae for the sample variance; see Homework 1.






Note



The recursive form reveals the new mean to be a convex combination of the old mean and the new observation. That is, it follows the form \(\alpha x + (1-\alpha) y\) for some coefficient \(\alpha \in [0,1]\).








WarningNumerical stability



Formulas for the sample variance must balance the difference between the sum of squares and squared sum. Mathematically, we can derive equivalent expressions that require a single pass through the data. Computationally, we must pay close attention to numerical instability [see @welford1962].





Large sums feature in various algorithms. Unfortunately, the order of summation can affect results even in relatively simple calculations. Indeed, there are various algorithms for computing
\[
\sum_{i=1}{n} x_{i} = x_{1} + x_{2} + \ldots + x_{n},
\]
because such calculations used to vary quite wildly due to the algorithm used, the programming language used, the underlying operating system, and, crucially, a machine’s hardware (think 1980s microcomputer era and beyond).
Mathematically, the sum of numbers is invariant to order of summation. Kahan-Babuška summation is a compensated algorithm which controls numerical errors due to loss of precision [see @kahan1965; comments from Wikipedia].

function sum_kb(x)
  T = eltype(x)
  result = zero(T) # Prepare the accumulator.
  c = zero(T)      # A running compensation for lost low-order bits.
  for i in eachindex(x)
    # c is zero the first time around
    y = x[i] - c
    # Alas, result is big, y small, so low-order digits of y are lost.
    t = result + y
    # (t - result) cancels the high-order part of y;
    # subtracting y recovers negative (low part of y).
    c = (t - result) - y
    # Algebraically, c should always be zero. Beware
    # overly-aggressive optimizing compilers!
    result = t
    # Next time around, the lost low part will be added to y
    # in a fresh attempt.
  end
  return result
end


function sum_direct(x)
  result = zero(eltype(x))
  for i in eachindex(x)
    result = result + x[i]
  end
  return result
end

Let’s see what happens with well-behaved inputs.

Random.seed!(206)
x = randn(10^3)
ref = sum(x) # reference solution


ref - sum_direct(x)


ref - sum_kb(x)

Now test against poorly-behaved inputs.

Random.seed!(206)
x = randn(10^6) .+ 1e9
ref = sum(x) # reference solution


ref - sum_direct(x)


ref - sum_kb(x)

Pairwise summation also takes a simple approach often described as divide and conquer.

function sum_pairwise(x)
  n = length(x)
  # base cases
  if n == 1
    return first(x)
  elseif n == 0
    return 0
  end
  m = div(n, 2) # Euclidean division
  s1 = @views sum_pairwise(x[1:m])     # delegate
  s2 = @views sum_pairwise(x[(m+1):n]) # delegate
  return s1 + s2
end


ref - sum_pairwise(x)

&= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} \\
s_{n}^{2}
&= \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{i} - \mu_{n})^{2}.
\end{align*}\]
We seek a method to update the sample estimates after receiving a new observation, \(x_{n+1}\). This presents a few issues:

If \(n\) is large (say \(\ge 10^{9}\)), then recomputing the estimates from scratch is wasteful.
Alternatively, we may be operating in a streaming setting in which we anticipate receiving many more additional observations in the future at unknown times.

With a bit of algebra, one can easily rewrite these formulas in a recursive form. For the sample mean we have
\[\begin{align*}
\mu_{n+1}
&=
\frac{1}{n+1} \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} x_{i} \\
&=
\frac{1}{n+1} \times \frac{n}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} + \frac{1}{n+1} x_{n+1} \\
&=
\frac{n}{n+1} \mu_{n} + \frac{1}{n+1} x_{n+1}.
\end{align*}\]
Given the current estimate \(\mu_{n}\), we can update the sample mean with the new observation \(x_{n+1}\). The key feature of this algorithm is that it is a one-pass procedure in which we use each data point once and only once. There are similar formulae for the sample variance; see Homework 1.






Note



The recursive form reveals the new mean to be a convex combination of the old mean and the new observation. That is, it follows the form \(\alpha x + (1-\alpha) y\) for some coefficient \(\alpha \in [0,1]\).








WarningNumerical stability



Formulas for the sample variance must balance the difference between the sum of squares and squared sum. Mathematically, we can derive equivalent expressions that require a single pass through the data. Computationally, we must pay close attention to numerical instability [see @welford1962].





Large sums feature in various algorithms. Unfortunately, the order of summation can affect results even in relatively simple calculations. Indeed, there are various algorithms for computing
\[
\sum_{i=1}{n} x_{i} = x_{1} + x_{2} + \ldots + x_{n},
\]
because such calculations used to vary quite wildly due to the algorithm used, the programming language used, the underlying operating system, and, crucially, a machine’s hardware (think 1980s microcomputer era and beyond).
Mathematically, the sum of numbers is invariant to order of summation. Kahan-Babuška summation is a compensated algorithm which controls numerical errors due to loss of precision [see @kahan1965; comments from Wikipedia].

function sum_kb(x)
  T = eltype(x)
  result = zero(T) # Prepare the accumulator.
  c = zero(T)      # A running compensation for lost low-order bits.
  for i in eachindex(x)
    # c is zero the first time around
    y = x[i] - c
    # Alas, result is big, y small, so low-order digits of y are lost.
    t = result + y
    # (t - result) cancels the high-order part of y;
    # subtracting y recovers negative (low part of y).
    c = (t - result) - y
    # Algebraically, c should always be zero. Beware
    # overly-aggressive optimizing compilers!
    result = t
    # Next time around, the lost low part will be added to y
    # in a fresh attempt.
  end
  return result
end


function sum_direct(x)
  result = zero(eltype(x))
  for i in eachindex(x)
    result = result + x[i]
  end
  return result
end

Let’s see what happens with well-behaved inputs.

Random.seed!(206)
x = randn(10^3)
ref = sum(x) # reference solution


ref - sum_direct(x)


ref - sum_kb(x)

Now test against poorly-behaved inputs.

Random.seed!(206)
x = randn(10^6) .+ 1e9
ref = sum(x) # reference solution


ref - sum_direct(x)


ref - sum_kb(x)

Pairwise summation also takes a simple approach often described as divide and conquer.

function sum_pairwise(x)
  n = length(x)
  # base cases
  if n == 1
    return first(x)
  elseif n == 0
    return 0
  end
  m = div(n, 2) # Euclidean division
  s1 = @views sum_pairwise(x[1:m])     # delegate
  s2 = @views sum_pairwise(x[(m+1):n]) # delegate
  return s1 + s2
end


ref - sum_pairwise(x)

title: Introduction to Algorithms
text:
Big O Notation
Given a problem dimension \(n\), we approximate the complexity of an algorithm by identifying the leading order behavior of how that complexity grows as a function of \(n\). For example, the complexity of computing the inner/dot product between two vector \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\):
\[
\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle
= \boldsymbol{x}^{\top} \boldsymbol{y}
= \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{i} y_{i}
= x_{1} y_{1} + x_{2} y_{2} + \ldots + x_{n} y_{n}
\]
can be calculated exactly by counting

\(n\) multiplication operations (1 for each pair of components),
\(n-1\) addition operations.

Hence, the number of flops is \(n + (n-1) = 2n-1\). Since \(n \ge 1\) in general, the leading order term can be said to be proportional to \(n\). This can be summarized with the Big O notation, \(\mathcal{O}(n)\). Note that Big O notation has a precise definition depending on whether it is used to describe the leading order behavior of a function, or the complexity of an algorithm; the latter uses a more restrictive definition.
Definition We say an algorithm is order \(\mathcal{O}(f(n))\) if the leading order of flops is \(c \times f(n)\).

Matrix-Vector Multiplication: Given \(\boldsymbol{A}\) \(m \times n\) and \(\boldsymbol{b}\) \(n \times 1\), the product \(\boldsymbol{A} \cdot \boldsymbol{b}\) requires \(2mn\) flops, or \(\mathcal{O}(mn)\) flops.
Matrix-Matrix Multiplication: Given the same \(\boldsymbol{A}\) and matrix \(\boldsymbol{B}\) \(n \times p\), \(\boldsymbol{A} \cdot \boldsymbol{B}\) requires 2mnp or \(\mathcal{O}(mnp)\) flops.

title: Introduction to Algorithms
text:
Hierarchy of Complexity
Let’s say a problem is size \(n\). Then:

Exponential order: \(\mathcal{O}(b^{n})\) (NP-hard; horrible!)
Polynomial order: \(\mathcal{O}(n^{q})\) (doable!)
“Superlinear” order: \(\mathcal{O}(n \log n)\) (fast)
Linear order: \(\mathcal{O}(n)\) (fast)
Log order: \(\mathcal{O}(\log n)\) (super fast)

Peter Huber gave the following classification of data sets



Data Size
Bytes
Storage Mode




Tiny
\(10^2\)
Piece of paper


Small
\(10^4\)
A few pieces of paper


Medium
\(10^6\) (megatbytes)
A floppy disk


Large
\(10^8\)
Hard disk


Huge
\(10^9\) (gigabytes)
Hard disk(s)


Massive
\(10^{12}\) (terabytes)
RAID storage



To appreciate the difference between \(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\) and \(\mathcal{O}(n\log n)\) on massive data, let’s suppose we have a teraflop supercomputer capable of doing \(10^{12}\) flops per second.

For a problem of size \(n=10^{12}\), an order \(\mathcal{O}(n \log n)\) algorithm takes about \(10^{12} \log (10^{12}) / 10^{12} \approx 27 \text{ seconds}.\)
An order \(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\) algorithm takes about \(10^{12}\) seconds, which is approximately 31710 years!

Our goal is to understand enough computational complexity that we, as statisticians/data scientists, can identify and select appropriate algorithms for different problems.

Data Scientist (n.): Person who is better at statistics than any software engineer and better at software engineering than any statistician.
— Josh Willis on Twitter

title: Introduction to Algorithms
text:
Computational complexity of vector operations
The flop count or operation count is the total number of flops in an algorithm.
A (very) crude predictor of run time of the algorithm is \[
\text{run time} \approx \frac{\text{flop count}}{\text{computer speed (flops/second)}}.
\]
Dominant term: the highest-order term in the flop count. \[
\frac 13 n^3 + 100 n^2 + 10n + 5 \approx \frac 13 n^3.
\]
Order: the power in the dominant term. \[
\frac 13 n^3 + 100 n^2 + 10n + 5 = \text{order } n^3 = \mathcal{O}(n^3).
\]

title: Refactoring Code
text:
What’s wrong with this code?

Not encapsulated: Re-run by cutting and pasting code, but how much of it? Also, the code is difficult to re-use and make part of something larger.
Inflexible: To change initial guess at \(a\), we have to edit, cut, paste, and re-run.
Error-prone: To change the data set, we have to edit, cut, paste, re-run, and hope that all the edits are consistent.
Hard to fix: should stop when the absolute value of derivative is small, but this stops when it is large and negative. Imagine having five copies of this and needing to fix same bug on each!

title: Databases
text:
What is SQL?
SQL (short for Structured Query Language) is a language for managing relational databases with structured data. Its purpose is to facilitate the storage, movement, and updating of data. The structured is less about the data and more about the approach; SQL is based on a mathematical model. Roughly speaking, the components of an SQL are:

Data Definition: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, RENAME
Data Manipulation: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
Data Control: GRANT, REVOKE
Transaction Control: COMMIT, REVOKE, ROLLBACK
Data Query: SELECT

In the schema above, there are several tables (airports, flights, and airlines for example) which are related to each other, but whose records do not quite fit together in a single object. For example, the airports table relates to the flights table in terms of the origin and destination fields, but the former contains additional pieces of information such as geographical coordinates. While longitude and latitude define an an origin and destination it is the airport itself that is relevant to flight information.
The relational aspect is due to the theoretical foundations of SQL and other database query languages: It uses relational algebra to define various operations on finite relations, which are defined in terms of tuples and attributes.






An attribute \(r_{j}\) is a name paired to a data type; it is a column in a table.
A tuple is an ordered set of attributes \(R = (r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{p})\); it is a row in a table.
A relation is a set of tuples \(\{R_{1}, R_{2}, \ldots, R_{n}\}\); it is a table. Order does not matter.

Here set is a mathematical set. Crucially, this means the names of each attribute must be unique. The purpose of strict, mathematical rigor in these definitions is to design a system that approximates first-order logic. A language based on such a model can be analyzed and understood.

Edgar F. Codd famously formalized the concept of a relational database while working at IBM in the 1970s.
Theory was used to design a system to implement various operations; e.g. renaming, selecting, joining.
The same theory can also be used to optimize queries, increasing execution speed.
If you want to master SQL, you must master relational algebra.
If you just need to use SQL, it is usually enough to understand the split-apply-combine strategy.

title: Databases
text:
What is SQLite?
SQL comes in many dialects. SQLite itself is a software library that acts as an engine for using SQL. We will use SQLite simply because it can be run in a server-less fashion – it just operates on files on our computer.
Note, however, that other SQL engines operate on a server model: connections to a database are typically between a client and server. Moreover, these systems in general must deal with concurrency – ensuring that multiple simultaneous updates to a database are resolved intelligently.

title: Databases
text:
Why bother?

You’re working with data that cannot fit neatly into a single file (e.g. a CSV) because it contains different types of entities (e.g. you actually have multiple tables).
Your data is changing/needs to be updated from possibly multiple sources.
You’re working in a distributed or streaming setting.
You need careful logging of how a database is accessed and updated to enforce certain properties. See also BASE and CAP Theorem.

… and many more compelling reasons. Performance or dealing with Big Data are not necessarily good use cases for SQL. At the end we’ll look at alternatives for those kinds of scenarios.

title: Databases
text:
Obtaining the Data
We installed the nycflights13 package in R and will now load it to make the various tables available (instead of manually downloading).

# R Code
library(nycflights13)
flights |> head(n = 10)

Now we’ll retrieve the tables on the Julia side.

# Back to Julia
flights = rcopy(R"flights")
weather = rcopy(R"weather")
planes = rcopy(R"planes")
airports = rcopy(R"airports")
airlines = rcopy(R"airlines")

first(flights, 10)

Note that columns with a ? next to the type information hint at explicitly missing values.

title: Databases
text:
Connecting to a Database
First we need to establish a connection to a database. This is done through SQLite.DB.

con = DBInterface.connect(SQLite.DB, "nycflights13.db")


If we provide an argument: The database lives in a file. Some RAM is used up as we interact with the database.
Otherwise: The entire database is stored in-memory, meaning you’ll use up RAM to store the entire database.
There are more generic options via URIs.

title: Databases
text:
Initialization

Starting from scratch
The CREATE TABLE statement allows us to instantiate a new table in our database. Then we can execute INSERT INTO statements to populate the table.

# Delete the table if it already exists
DBInterface.execute(con, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS airports")

# Then proceed with our example
DBInterface.execute(con,
  "CREATE TABLE airports (faa TEXT, name TEXT, lat REAL, lon REAL, alt REAL, tz INT, dst TEXT, tzone TEXT)"
)
DBInterface.execute(con,
  "INSERT INTO airports VALUES ('04G', 'Lansdowne Airport', 41.1, -80.6, 1044, -5, 'A', 'America/New_York')" 
)

Most SQL interface packages will return a cursor that allows the caller to iterate over the relations returned by an executed query. The CREATE TABLE and INSERT INTO statements do not return relations, so we’ll turn to SELECT * FROM for an example:

for row in DBInterface.execute(con, "SELECT * FROM airports")
  attrs = propertynames(row)
  foreach(attr -> println("$(attr): $(getproperty(row, attr))"), attrs)
end


propertynames(row) gives us the attributes for the particular relation (row).
getproperty(row, attr) returns the value for the specified attribute attr.
If we already know the attribute names, we could just as easily write (Julia) code like row.faa or row[1] instead.

Alternatively, we can pipe |> the cursor to table-like types (i.e. that implement the Tables.jl specification) to display our results:

DBInterface.execute(con, "SELECT * FROM airports") |> DataFrame



Loading from a source
First let’s clear the database for the sake of our example.

tablenames = ["flights", "weather", "planes", "airports", "airlines"]
for tablename in tablenames
  DBInterface.execute(con, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS $(tablename)")
end

Now load it. DBInterface.jl does not provide an abstraction for this, so we’ll have to use an SQLite.jl command directly:

SQLite.load!(flights, con, "flights")
SQLite.load!(weather, con, "weather")
SQLite.load!(planes, con, "planes")
SQLite.load!(airports, con, "airports")
SQLite.load!(airlines, con, "airlines")

Display the tables available in the database by querying the schema:

DBInterface.execute(con, """
SELECT
  name
FROM
  sqlite_master
WHERE
  type = 'table' AND
  name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'
""") |> DataFrame

If you replace name above with *, you will be able to see every column in the database schema.

type : index or table.
name : index or table name
tbl_name : Name of the table
rootpage : internal information to SQLite.
sql : The SQL statement which would create the given table.

title: Databases
text:
SELECT
SELECT columns or computations
  FROM table
  WHERE condition
  GROUP BY columns
  HAVING condition
  ORDER BY column [ASC | DESC]
  LIMIT offset, count;
Display the carrier, flight number, origin, and destination of every flight:

example(con, """
SELECT carrier, flight, tailnum, origin, dest
  FROM flights
""")

Display the flights table (all columns) but limited to 10 rows.

example(con, "SELECT * FROM flights LIMIT 10")


first(flights, 10) # DataFrames.jl equivalent

Ditto, but order the relations according to the arr_delay attribute.

example(con, "SELECT * FROM flights ORDER BY arr_delay LIMIT 10")


first(sort(flights, :arr_delay), 10)

Ditto, but do it in descending order.

example(con, "SELECT * FROM flights ORDER BY arr_delay DESC LIMIT 10")


first(sort(flights, :arr_delay, rev = true), 10)

title: Databases
text:
WHERE
Filtering can be achieved using this keyword. Let’s identify the flights with at least 2 hour arrival delays and negative departure delays (early departure). It is at this level of complexity that one starts to see possible performance differences so let’s do some light benchmarking, too.

@time begin
  example(con, """SELECT origin, dest, arr_delay, dep_delay
    FROM flights
    WHERE arr_delay >= 120 AND dep_delay < 0
  """)
end

Most DataFrame-like implementations use eager evaluation, meaning many temporary copies are created in executing complex queries.

@time begin
  tmp1 = dropmissing(flights)
  tmp2 = filter("arr_delay" => >=(120), tmp1)
  tmp3 = filter("dep_delay" => <(0), tmp2)
  select(tmp3, ["origin", "dest", "arr_delay", "dep_delay"])
end

We can do a little better by executing the subset before filtering, leveraging mutation, and fusing the filter operations:

# avoid performance penalty by using a non-anonymous function
is_interesting(arr_delay, dep_delay) = arr_delay >= 120 && dep_delay < 0

@time begin
  tmp1 = dropmissing(flights)
  select!(tmp1, ["origin", "dest", "arr_delay", "dep_delay"])
  filter!([:arr_delay, :dep_delay] => is_interesting, tmp1)
end

Takeaway message

If your SQL engine has a query optimizer, it’s worth learning how to use it if you’re working with huge databases + queries.
You generally cannot control how an SQL engine evaluates your queries, but they’ll try to do the “right” thing. A programming language usually exposes tools in the language to achieve just that.

title: Databases
text:
Computations
SQL dialects usually offer some support for basic arithmetic and descriptive statistics.

example(con, """
SELECT distance, air_time, distance / air_time AS speed
  FROM flights
  ORDER BY speed DESC LIMIT 10
""")

title: Databases
text:
GROUP BY, HAVING

Aggregate relations with GROUP BY
Pre-aggregation selection with WHERE
Post-aggregation selection with HAVING


example(con, """
SELECT dest, AVG(arr_delay) AS mean_arr_delay 
  FROM flights
  WHERE arr_delay > 0
  GROUP BY dest
  HAVING mean_arr_delay > 60
""")

title: Databases
text:
JOIN
SELECT * FROM x INNER JOIN y USING (z)
SELECT * FROM x LEFT OUTER JOIN y USING (z)
SELECT * FROM x RIGHT OUTER JOIN y USING (z)
SELECT * FROM x FULL OUTER JOIN y USING (z)

example(con, """
SELECT year, month, day, carrier, flight
  FROM flights INNER JOIN airlines
  USING(carrier)
""")

The USING (z) clause can be replaced by

The ON x.z == y.z clause, which allows different key column names, and relations will be filtered before joining.
The WHERE x.z == y.z clause, where relations will be filtered after a join has taken place.


example(con, """
SELECT year, month, day, carrier, flight, origin, dest
  FROM flights
  INNER JOIN airports
    ON flights.dest == airports.faa 
  WHERE flights.origin == "JFK"
    AND airports.tz <= -8
""")

title: Databases
section: Data does not fit in memory
text:
Data does not fit in memory
Do you really need to load the full data into RAM? If not, you have a few options.

Use memory-mapped options
Memory-mapped solutions use disk space instead of RAM.


Store the data in binary formats
The Parquet, Arrow, and HDF5 file types are available in Python, R, and Julia.

Arrow.write("flights.arrow", flights)

For example, Arrow provides a memory-mapped solution to reading tabular data:

arrow_flights = Arrow.Table("flights.arrow")

Dataframe-like libraries also tend to support compressed file formats (e.g. zip or gz), which may be combined with memory-mapped solutions.

CSV.write("flights.csv.gz", flights; compress = true)



Chunk your data
Consider partitioning your data source into chunks; e.g. separate files. Some Dataframe-like libraries provide support with chunking without manually partitioning the data:

# Read approx 10,000 items in 4 chunks.
chunks = CSV.Chunks("flights.csv.gz"; limit = 10^4, ntasks = 4)

for (k, file) in enumerate(chunks)
  df = DataFrame(file)
  display(describe(df))
end

title: Databases
section: Data does not consist of relations
text:
Data does not consist of relations
Numerical experiments generate data. Large-scale experiments may yield “big data” but it need not be tabular; e.g. a custom type. [Serialization] tools like JLD2.jl offer a way to save and load your data in its native format, using both compression and memory-mapping.
Similar tools exists in Python (e.g. pickle) and R (e.g. RDS for single objects and RDA for multiple objects)

struct MyType{T}
  data::T
end


MyType(1.0)


MyType([1,2,3])


JLD2.save_object("example.jld2", MyType([1, 2, 3]))


JLD2.load_object("example.jld2")

title: Cross Validation
text:
using RDatasets
using LinearAlgebra, Random
using Statistics, StatsBase, Distributions
using DataFrames, Plots, StatsPlots, LaTeXStrings

title: Cross Validation
text:
Validation Approach

Randomly split data into a training set to build your model, and a holdout set to validate the fitted model.
Carry out the estimation procedure using the training set.
Evalute the model’s performance using the holdout set.


function train_test_split(y, X, at)
  n = length(y)
  idx = randperm(n)       # "shuffle" the data
  i = round(Int, n * at)  # split at this index
  train = (y[idx[1:i]], X[idx[1:i], :])
  test = (y[idx[i+1:end]], X[idx[i+1:end], :])
  return train, test
end


function validate(y, X, λgrid, score; intercept = false, at = 0.5, kwargs...)
  score_vals = zeros(length(λgrid))
  (y_train, X_train), (y_test, X_test) = train_test_split(y, X, at)
  for (k, λ) in enumerate(λgrid)
    βλ = coordinate_descent(y_train, X_train, λ; intercept = intercept, kwargs...)
    score_vals[k] += score(y_test, X_test, βλ, λ, intercept)
  end
  # identify the 'best' model
  idx = argmin(score_vals)
  λ, best_score = λgrid[idx], score_vals[idx]
  return λ, best_score
end


λgrid = 10 .^ range(-3, 3, step = 0.5)
validate(y, X, λgrid, score_loss; at = 0.5)

title: Cross Validation
text:
Leave-One-Out

Starting from \(i = 1\), use exclude \((x_{i}, y_{i})\) from your data.
Use the remaining \(n-1\) data points to fit your model.
Evaluate the model on the holdout data \((x_{i}, y_{i})\)
Increment \(i\), select the next \((x_{i}, y_{i})\), and go back to Step 2.


function loocv(y, X, λgrid, score; intercept = false, kwargs...)
  idx = ones(Bool, length(y))
  score_vals = zeros(length(λgrid))
  for i in eachindex(y)
    # exclude the i-th datum
    idx[i] = false
    y_train, X_train = @views y[idx], X[idx, :]

    # evaluate models with training set
    for (k, λ) in enumerate(λgrid)
      βλ = coordinate_descent(y_train, X_train, λ; intercept = intercept, kwargs...)
      score_vals[k] += score(y[i], X[i, :], βλ, λ, intercept) / n # averaging score over all LOOCV holdout sets
    end
    idx[i] = true
  end
  # identify the 'best' model
  idx = argmin(score_vals)
  λ, best_score = λgrid[idx], score_vals[idx]
  return λ, best_score
end


λgrid = 10 .^ range(-3, 3, step = 1.0)
loocv(y, X, λgrid, score_loss)

title: Cross Validation
text:
\(K\)-Fold
Generalizes the leave-one-out approach; it is a special case of \(K\)-fold with \(K = 1\).

Randomly split the data into \(K\) groups of roughly equal sizes called a fold.
Reserve the first fold for validation.
Fit the data on the remaining \(K-1\) folds.
Evaluate the model’s performance on the validation set.
Repeat from Step 3 for the next fold until all \(K\) are exhausted.


function kfoldcv(y, X, λgrid, score; K = 5, intercept = false, kwargs...)
  n = length(y)
  idx = round.(Int, range(1, n, K+1)) # indices for computing folds
  score_vals = zeros(length(λgrid))
  for fold in 1:K
    idxval = idx[fold]:idx[fold+1]
    idxtrain = setdiff(1:n, idxval)
    y_train, X_train = y[idxtrain], X[idxtrain, :]
    y_test, X_test = y[idxval], X[idxval, :]
    # evaluate models with training set
    for (k, λ) in enumerate(λgrid)
      βλ = coordinate_descent(y_train, X_train, λ; intercept = intercept, kwargs...)
      score_vals[k] += score(y_test, X_test, βλ, λ, intercept) / K
    end
  end
  # identify the 'best' model
  idx = argmin(score_vals)
  λ, best_score = λgrid[idx], score_vals[idx]
  return λ, best_score
end


λgrid = 10 .^ range(-3, 3, step = 1.0)
kfoldcv(y, X, λgrid, score_loss; K = 5)

The \(K\)-fold strategy tends to have smaller variance compared to Leave-One-Out. Why?

Leave-One-Out effectively fits \(n\) models which see nearly identical training data.
As such, any model errors/scores will tend to be highly correlated. Estimated metrics are thus highly variable.
\(K\)-fold approach only fits \(K\) models which are fit on slightly overlapping data, decreasing correlation.
Unfortunately, \(K\)-fold still pays a price: higher bias. Cross validation techniqes are generally subject to bias-variance tradeoffs.

title: Cross Validation
text:
Nested / Repeated

Split data into training and testing.
Further split the training data into actual training and validation; e.g. using \(K\)-fold.
Select the best model using the validation set.
Evaluate the model on the testing set.


Should ameloriate the bias-variance tradeoff phenomenon, since the test set is never used for training (weaker correlation to training data).
More computationally expensive.

Can repeat any cross validation procedure in a Monte Carlo fashion to aid in assessing stability; e.g. in model selection or hyperparameter tuning.

title: Bootstrap
text:
using RCall
using RDatasets
using LinearAlgebra, Random
using Statistics, StatsBase, Distributions
using DataFrames, Plots, StatsPlots, LaTeXStrings

title: Bootstrap
text:
Why the name?

The “bootstrap” is a cute name for a vast generalization of the plug-in principle.
The name comes from the cliche “pull oneself up by one’s bootstraps” which although it describes a literal impossibility actually means succeed by one’s own efforts.
In statistics, the hint of impossibility is part of the flavor.
Seems problematic, but it (usually) works.

title: Bootstrap
text:
Resampling

The notation \(X_1^*, \dots, X_n^*\) IID \(\hat{F}_n\) means \(X_1^*, \dots, X_n^*\) are independent and identically distributed from the empirical distribution of the real data.
Sampling from the empirical distribution is just like sampling from a finite population, where the “population” is the real data \(X_1, \dots, X_n\).

To be IID sampling it must be done with replacement.
\(X_1^*, \dots, X_n^*\) are a sample with replacement from \(X_1, \dots, X_n\).
This is known as resampling.

title: Bootstrap
text:
Motivation for bootstrap

We want to know the sampling distribution of \(\hat{\theta}_n\) or \(\hat{\theta}_n - \theta\) or \(\frac{\hat{\theta}_n - \theta}{s(\hat{F}_n)}\).
This sampling distribution depends on the true unknown distribution \(F\) of the real data.
May be very difficult or impossible to calculate theoretically.
Even asymptotic approximation may be difficult if the parameter \(\theta = h(F)\) is a sufficiently complicated function of the true unknown \(F\).

Enter the “bootstrap world”:

In the “bootstrap world” everything is known, \(\hat{F}_n\) plays the role of the true unknown distribution and \(\hat{\theta}_n\) plays the role of the true unknown parameter value
The sampling distribution of \(\theta_n^*\) or \(\theta_n^* - \hat{\theta}_n\) or \(\frac{\theta_n^* - \hat{\theta}_n}{s(F_n^*)}\) may still be difficult to calculate theoretically, but it can always be “calculated” by simulation.

title: Bootstrap
text:
When it works

Much folklore about the bootstrap is misleading.
The bootstrap is large sample, approximate, asymptotic.

It is not an exact method.

The bootstrap analogy works when the empirical distribution \(\hat{F}_n\) is close to the true unknown distribution \(F\).

Usually the case when the sample size \(n\) is large and not otherwise.

title: Bootstrap
text:
Bootstrap percentile intervals

Simplest method of making confidence intervals for the unknown parameter is to take \(\alpha/2\) and \(1 - \alpha/2\) quantiles of the bootstrap distribution of the estimator \(\theta_n^*\) as endpoints of the 100(1 − \(\alpha\))% confidence interval.
Percentile method only makes sense when there is a symmetrizing transformation (some function of \(\hat{\theta}\) has an approximately symmetric distribution with the center of symmetry being the true unknown parameter value \(\theta\)).
The symmetrizing transformation does not have to be known, but it does have to exist.

title: Bootstrap
text:
Applying the bootstrap

State null and alternative hypotheses: \[
H_0: \mu = 33.02 \text{ versus } H_a: \mu \ne 33.02
\]
Choose a significance level. in our case \(\alpha = 0.05\).
Choose a test statistic. Since we wish to estimate the mean speed we can use the sample average.
Find the observed value of the test statistic.
Calculate a \(p\)-value?


mean(speed)

title: Bootstrap
text:
Where’s the sampling distribution?

We now need a \(p\)-value, but we don’t have the sampling distribution of our test statistic when the null hypothesis is true!
It is approximately normal, but that is a poor approximation here.
Instead we can perform a simulation under conditions in which we know the null hypothesis is true.
Use our data to represent the population, but first we shift it over so that the mean really is 33.02.


newspeed = speed .- mean(speed) .+ 33.02

fig = histogram(speed, xlabel = "Speed",
  layout = grid(1, 2),
  title = "Data", subplot = 1,
  size = (800, 400),
  legend = false
)
histogram!(newspeed, xlabel = "Speed", title = "Bootstrap Population", subplot = 2, legend = false)
fig

The histogram of newspeed will have exactly the same shape as speed, but will be shifted. In the bootstrap world, this is the “true” distribution.

title: Bootstrap
text:
Resampling

Now we reach into our fake population and take out 20 observations at random, with replacement.
We take out 20 because that’s the size of our initial sample.
We calculate the average and save it, then repeat this process many, many times.
Now we have a sampling distribution with mean 33.02!
Can compare this to our observed sample average and obtain a \(p\)-value.


function resample(data)
  sample(data, length(data), replace = true)
end


Random.seed!(1903)
n = 1000
bstrap = [mean(resample(newspeed)) for _ in 1:n]

fig = histogram(bstrap, title="Bootstrap Sampling Distribution", xlabel="Bootstrap Samples", legend = false)
vline!([mean(speed)], color = :red, lw = 2)
fig


Doesn’t look normal, which means we did the right thing.
Not impossible for the sample average to be 21.75.
But it’s not all that common, either.
What is the statistic in our bootstrap procedure?
Why do we highlight the value 21.75?

title: Bootstrap
text:
Defining the \(p\)-value

The \(p\)-value is the probability of obtaining a statistic “more extreme” than what we observed.
Notice \(21.75\) is \(33.02 - 21.75 = 11.27\) units away from the null hypothesis.
So the \(p\)-value is the probability of being more than 11.27 units away from 33.02.


μ = mean(newspeed)
Δ = abs(μ - mean(speed))
(μ - Δ, μ + Δ)


(sum(bstrap .< μ - Δ) + sum(bstrap .> μ + Δ)) / n

Since our significance level is 5%, we have evidence against \(H_0\) and conclude that Newcomb’s measurements were not consistent with the currently accepted figure.

title: Bootstrap
text:
Two-sample \(t\)-test

The two sample \(t\)-test checks for differences in means according to a known null distribution.
Similar to permutation tests.
Let’s resample and generate the sampling distribution under the bootstrap assumption.


function diff_in_means(data)
  muA = mean(data[data.Group .== "1", "Extra"])
  muB = mean(data[data.Group .== "2", "Extra"])
  return muA - muB
end

function resample(data::DataFrame)
  idx = resample(1:nrow(data))
  return data[idx, :]
end


Random.seed!(1903)

#
# H0: difference is centered at 0. Do this by centering groups at a common value.
#
x = sleep[sleep.Group .== "1", "Extra"]
x = x .- mean(x)
y = sleep[sleep.Group .== "2", "Extra"]
y = y .- mean(y)
newsleep = DataFrame(Extra = [x; y], Group = sleep.Group, ID = sleep.ID)
diff_in_means(newsleep)

# bootstrap
n = 2000
resample_diffs = [diff_in_means(resample(newsleep)) for _ in 1:n]

histogram(resample_diffs, title = "Bootstrap Sampling Distribution")
vline!([diff_in_means(sleep)], color = :red, lw = 3)


State the null and alternative hypothesis for the mean effect of the two drugs.
What is the value of the true parameter under the bootstrap?
State the condition needed for a valid \(p\)-value under \(H_0\).


(sum(resample_diffs .< -1.58) + sum(resample_diffs .> 1.58)) / n

title: Bootstrap
text:
Bootstrapping a single statistic

Can use the bootstrap to generate a 95% confidence interval for \(R^2\).
Linear regression of miles per gallon (mpg) on car weight (wt) and displacement (disp).
Data source is mtcars.
The bootstrapped confidence interval is based on 1000 replicates.


# Function to compute statistic
rsq <- function(formula, data, indices) {
  d <- data[indices,]  
  fit <- lm(formula, data=d)
  return(summary(fit)$r.square)
} 

# R^2 from the data
rsq(mpg ~ wt + disp, mtcars, 1:nrow(mtcars))

# Run the bootstrap
set.seed(206)
results <- boot(
  data = mtcars,
  statistic = rsq, 
  R = 1000,
  formula = mpg ~ wt + disp
)
results |> print()
NULL

Note that results has class boot.

boot.ci(results, type="bca") |> print()
NULL

title: The Unix Shell
text:
What is Unix?
UNIX is a broad term for a collection of operating systems that no longer exist. These systems emerged in the late 1960s/1970s when time-sharing was an important computing model. Its various projects represent tight collaboration between academic circles and industrial research groups (e.g. Bell Labs).
Although extinct, UNIX spawned descendant UNIX-like, or Linux-like, systems and continues to influence computing to this day. Part of its lasting impact is, arguably, due to the so-called UNIX Philosophy

Write programs that do one thing and do it well.
Write programs to work together.
Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
What is a Shell?
In the last several decades, humans have interacted with computers in a variety of ways. You are likely reading this on a graphical user interface (GUI). While appealing and (usually) intuitive, GUIs do not scale well to certain tasks. A command-line interace (CLI) is often an efficient interaction mode for manipulating files on computers and automating various repetitive tasks. Both GUIs and CLIs are examples of shells: they are user interfaces that allow an entity to interact with an OS.
In this class, we will use shell as a shorthand for CLI shell, which operate through text-based inputs and outputs. The class Docker image has three shells:

zsh: Z shell, which is the default. This default is used by modern MacOS, too. It is a good option for interactive work.
bash: Bourne Again Shell. It is a good option for scripting because it respects portability and adheres to well-established standards.
sh: Bourne Shell. This is the standard for system-level work and operations, and will not be relevant to us.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
But… why?
While CLIs have a learning curve that involve learning various commands, they also:

allow simple operations to be combined, forming new, useful programs,
allow commands to be recorded for documentaion, reuse, modification, and automation,
allow programs to be parameterized, extending their use, and
empower the user to be thoughtful, independent, competent, and fast.

title: The Unix Shell

Getting started
The class Docker image creates a container that, by default, will log you in to an interactive shell zsh. You will be greeted by a prompt:

The prompt is fully customizable, but this was chosen to present some information to students in the class:

@STAT206: A visual cue that you are in the container, not your own operating system’s environment.
~: The current directory. It is shorthand for your home directory, /home/student. The display will change as you navigate to different locations.
$: A visual cue that you may enter a command.

This brings up two important concepts to keep in mind (regardless of what computer/OS you use):

Everything you do on a computer, you do as a particular user. Users have different permissions that limit or enable access to resources on a computer.
Every command you type into your shell operates within some context, namely the directory you are currently in.







WarningNever use sudo unless it is absolutely necessary



In the past, many programmers would scour StackOverflow and similar websites to figure how to do something on their favorite Linux distro. There is a long tradition of trolling inexperienced users and plenty of misinformation.
Today, a Chat Bot may tell you to use sudo to implement a task you’re struggling to figure out.
Regardless of the source, it has been my experience (and the advice of countless experts) that sudo is almost never needed. Everything in this course has been set up so that you do not need to use it. Avoid running sudo commands on your computer unless you’re willing to accept the consequences.

Goals

Develop an understanding and appreciation of Git and version control.
Understand the difference between a local and remote repository.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
What is Version Control?

An article about computational science in a scientific publication is not the scholarship itself, it is merely the advertising of the scholarship. The actual scholarship is the complete software development environment and the complete set of instructions which generated the figures.

— Buckheit and Donoho (1995), summarizing Jon Claerbout’s ideas on reproducible research in computational sciences.
Researchers (Data Scientists, and other professionals) often need to manage a number of documents:

manuscripts/technical reports
notes
data
images
code
scripts

Today, many of those documents live on a computer.

Tracking different versions of a document by hand is tedious and error-prone.
Tracking the history of a changing document is cumbersome.

Version control has its origins in software development and has increasingly been adopted across various disciplines, including data science.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
What is Git?


A tool for distributed version control.
Originally developed by Linus Torvaldis for managing the Linux kernel.
Multiple people own and can edit copies of a repository.
Git operates on changes between versions of a document, effectively tracking line-by-line changes.
Each version of the repository exists as a commit, or snapshot.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
The model
Git keeps track of versions for various files, along with a log that tells us about why things changed.






working directory: the directory on your machine that represents your repository of files under version control.

These are just the files and directories that make up a project. There is no history or version control history.

staging area: files that you tag to commit changes are said to be staged / in the staging area.
local repo: your local repository; the collection of all the files in your folder + changes + history.

This consists only of your commits. Any changes/edits to files not committed are not in the local repository.
Your commits are linked to each other. This lets us go back in time to a different state of the working directory.

remote repo: a foreign version that lives elsewhere; usually a backup on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
commit: a snapshot of the project. This consists of specific files that were added/removed/edited + an informative message by the commit author.

The main idea is that git helps you put your projects under version control by examining your working tree, comparing to the local repo, and informing you of changes that have occurred. It is then incumbent on YOU to manage those changes and move them onto the staging area to be organized into commits stored in the local repo.






NoteBranches in Git



Git allows you to maintain multiple versions of the same workspace with separate commits using branches. By default, Git initializes your local repository with a main or master branch.
We will revisit branching much later in the course when we start using Git to collaborate with others.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
Basic commands
The list below is by no means exhaustive.

git init
This initializes a working directory as a local Git repository. Specifically, it creates a .git directory to store the history and metadata about various files in the repository.


git add <name of a file or directory>
Adds files to the staging area so that you can create a commit.


git commit
Opens an editor to draft a message associated with your proposed commit. This command supports various additional options.

Add the message in-line: git commit -m "This is my commit message"
Edit the previous commit: git commit --amend
Edit the previous commit, without updating the message: git commit --amend --no-edit



git status
Check that state of the repository. This will highlight any files that have been edited, any that are not tracked, and any that might already be staged.


git log
Explore the local repository’s history.


git diff
Compare differences across commits.


git push
Upload the work on your local repository to a remote repository.


git fetch / git pull
Download the work on a remote repository to your local repository.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
Writing a commit message

The next person to read your work in 6 months is not going to be some schmuck. It’s going to be YOU!

— A certain UCR Statistics Professor
Treat commit messages like entries in a journal. They are meant to be read by someone. There are two parts of a commit message:

The first line: A succinct summary. This is what gets displayed in most Git tools; e.g. on GitHub.
The rest: Add additional lines to add more context. A commit message can be as long as you want. Use it!

title: Version Control with Git
text:
A basic single user workflow

Using Git for the first time on a new computer

Set up your identity in Git. See Lab 0 on how to configure Git.
Consider setting up a global .gitignore.
Set up SSH access to your GitHub/GitLab/Other Git Service for the new machine.



Setting up a new project

Create the main project directory and cd into it.
Run git init.
Set up the project with some basic files so you can create an initial commit. For example, adding a README.md is a good first step especially if you plan to host the project on GitHub.
Set up a remote repository, if applicable.
Run git add ... and git commit ... to create the first commit in the project.
Push the initial commit to the remote repository.



Working on a project

Run git status to check for local changes. Run git fetch --all to check for remote changes.

If your remote repo has changes, consider whether you can git pull them.

Edit some file(s), working towards The Next Logical Step.

This should be implementing some small part of your project. For example, writing a specific function that your project requires can be The Next Logical Step.
At The Next Logical Step, the project should be in a semi-working state.
In the early phase of a project, that might mean that you’ve worked out enough to test basic functionality.
For example, you might write a script or function to load a dataset and print some summary statistics.

Run git add ... to organize files and changes associated with The Next Logical Step.
Write an informative message about what was done and any useful context.

D. Computing \(\mathbf{Q}\)
The last part shows that we can put \(\mathbf{X}\) into upper triangular form using a sequence of Householder transformations. But what happened to the matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\)? One can show that

\mathbf{Q}^\top = \mathbf{H}_{p} \mathbf{H}_{p-1} \cdots \mathbf{H}_2 \mathbf{H}_1,

Computational efficiency, in terms of speed and memory, is a key criterion in grading this assignment.



Overview
Nonnegative matrix factorization (NNMF) was introduced by Lee and Seung (1999) as an alternative to principal components and vector quantization. This method appeared in the past (Lawton and Sylvestre, 1971) as a technique for determining the shape of two overlapping functions via additive mixtures. Today, NNMF has applications in data compression, clustering, and deconvolution.






Figure 1: Illustration of NNMF



In mathematical terms, the goal of NNMF is to approximate a data matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) with nonnegative entries \(x_{ij}\) as a product of two low-rank matrices \(\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}\) and \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n}\), also with nonnegative entries \(v_{ik}\) and \(w_{kj}\). That is, one chooses \(r < \min\{m,n\}\) so that the rank of \(\mathbf{V}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) is at most \(r\). We fit/estimate the factors \(\mathbf{V}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) by minimizing the squared Frobenius norm of the residuals matrix \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{V} \mathbf{W}\), \[
L(\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}) = \|\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{V} \mathbf{W}\|_{\text{F}}^2 = \sum_i \sum_j \left(x_{ij} - \sum_k v_{ik} w_{kj} \right)^2, \quad v_{ik} \ge 0, w_{kj} \ge 0,
\] which should lead to a good factorization. Lee and Seung suggest an iterative algorithm with multiplicative updates \[
v_{ik}^{(t+1)} = v_{ik}^{(t)} \frac{\sum_j x_{ij} w_{kj}^{(t)}}{\sum_j b_{ij}^{(t)} w_{kj}^{(t)}}, \quad \text{where } b_{ij}^{(t)} = \sum_k v_{ik}^{(t)} w_{kj}^{(t)},
\] \[
w_{kj}^{(t+1)} = w_{kj}^{(t)} \frac{\sum_i x_{ij} v_{ik}^{(t+1)}}{\sum_i b_{ij}^{(t+1/2)} v_{ik}^{(t+1)}}, \quad \text{where } b_{ij}^{(t+1/2)} = \sum_k v_{ik}^{(t+1)} w_{kj}^{(t)}
\] that will drive the objective \(L^{(t)} = L(\mathbf{V}^{(t)}, \mathbf{W}^{(t)})\) downhill. Superscript \(t\) indicates the iteration number.

text:
Goals

Understand the organizational structure of a file system on Linux.
Understand relative and absolute paths.
Develop awareness of key locations on a Linux system and the class Docker image.
Understand that programs, regardless of operating system, operate in a context.

title: The File System
text:
Overview
Files on computers are generally arranged in a hierarchical manner, specifically as a rooted tree. The following is the output of tree -L 1 / on a machine with macOS Sequoia. This command displays a file system, one level deep, starting from the root directory /:
/
├── Applications
├── bin
├── cores
├── dev
├── etc -> private/etc
├── home -> /System/Volumes/Data/home
├── Library
├── opt
├── private
├── sbin
├── System
├── tmp -> private/tmp
├── Users
├── usr
├── var -> private/var
└── Volumes

17 directories, 0 files
Everything is a file in the Unix world, yet the output above clearly distinguishes between files and directories. Files are data on your computer. Directories are, too, but their role is to act as folders connecting one level of a tree to other parts in the system. In brief, directories are branches and files are leaves in the rooted tree structure.






ImportantSymbolic Links



You might notice a few of the labels in the tree output above have arrows; for example home -> /System/Volumes/Data/home. These are examples of symbolic links, which are files that point to a location elsewhere. Symbolic links are useful for introducing indirection and decoupling an interface from an implementation.

Indirection, as a concept, can be useful for creating shortcuts. For example, say you have multiple projects that need access to a particular resource nested deeply within your file system. A single symbolic link can provide access at a convenient location and allow each project to inherit access without writing out cumbersome paths.
To give another example, symbolic links can be used to manage versions of a resource. If two projects need access to two versions of FANCY_DATASET, each project can use its own symbolic link FANCY_DATASET which points to the appropriate version. This simplifies any scripts operating on that resource without having to introduce version information into the code.



The following is mock output of tree on a directory named repo. Your Git repository for this class will resemble this structure over time.
repo/
├── hw/
│   ├── hw1/
│   │   ├── complex_data.arrow
│   │   ├── fancy_algorithm.py
│   │   ├── report.qmd
│   │   ├── environment.yml
│   │   └── <other code or files>
│   ├── hw2/
│   │
│   ...
│   └── hw8/
└── labs/
    ├── lab1/
    │   ├── report.qmd
    │   ├── environment.yml
    │   └── test.py
    ...
    └── lab8
Here repo/ is the top level, so we can say these files are rooted at repo/, but it is not the root directory. The root directory is unique because Unix/Linux file systems are generally rooted trees. By definition, there can only be one root that serves as the absolute top level.

title: The File System
text:
Absolute vs Relative Paths
Virtually every operating system operates on file paths. A file path is a sequence of names/labels of specific files/directories in a file system that point to a specific location. On Linux, file paths are formatted by the file separator /. Let’s revisit the repo/ example:
repo/
├── hw/
│   ├── hw1/
│   │   ├── complex_data.arrow
│   │   ├── fancy_algorithm.py
│   │   ├── report.qmd
│   │   ├── environment.yml
│   │   └── <other code or files>
│   ├── hw2/
...

The file path repo/ leads from wherever repo/ exists to repo/. Equivalently, ./repo.
The file path repo/hw is similar, but points one directory down towards hw/. Equivalently, ./repo/hw.
The file path repo/hw/hw1/report.qmd is a file path that leads from wherever repo/ exists to report.qmd. Equivalently, ./reop/hw/hw1/report.qmd.

All these examples are relative paths because they depend on context. That context is ., a symbolic file path that points here which is wherever you might be. From here you can reference the parent directory using .. which is whatever the parent might be.
In contrast, absolute paths do not depend on context because they’re absolute! On a Linux system, /repo/hw/hw1/report.qmd is an example of an absolute path (that probably does not exist). Let’s modify the example so that repo/ resides inside a stat206/ directory somewhere on the file system:
/
├──Documents
│   └──stat206
│       └── repo
...         ├── hw
            │   ├── hw1/
            │   │   ├── complex_data.arrow
            │   │   ├── fancy_algorithm.py
            │   │   ├── report.qmd
            │   │   ├── environment.yml
            │   │   └── <other code or files>
            │   ├── hw2/
            ...
Here /Documents/stat206/repo/ is an absolute path that references repo. On Linux, all absolute paths must begin with the root directory, /. This eliminates any ambiguity.

Use in Programming and Data Analysis
In practice, we rarely, if ever, use absolute paths. Relative paths are preferred because two machines rarely share the same structure in their file systems. This is all the more relevant if we consider machines that have completely different operating systems. We conclude with the following advice that ought to ring true in many contexts.

Be thoughtful about how you organize files for a project. Stick to conventions, where possible, and aim for simplicity whenever guidance is scarce.
Prepend your file paths with . and .. to communicate your intent in references. It might help you or other catch mistakes.
Place scripts close to the top level of a project’s directory. This often simplifies relative paths.
Avoid hard-coding file separators into your code source files. Most programming languages provide tools to handle file separators correctly across operating systems.







ImportantAside: What about Windows?




There is no “root directory” in Windows, at least not in the same sense as Unix-like file systems. Windows file systems use drive letters as the root node; for example, the C:\ drive. Unix-like/Linux-like systems support working with multiple drives, too, but do not anchor their file systems to specific drives.
Windows uses the backslash \ as a file separator. It is one of the reasons (but not the only reason) we cannot hard-code file paths in scripts.

title: The File System
section: Special Locations on Linux File Systems
text:
Special Locations on Linux File Systems
Most operating systems exploit the hierarchical nature of file systems to organize sensitive information and tools so that permission settings can readily provide a level of security. The following are useful locations for you to be aware about:

/: The root directory. User accounts typically do not have file permissions here, and you should keep it that way.
/usr: Home to user-level resources. These are common to all users on a machine.

/usr/bin: Home to essential binaries, or programs, for the operating system. Commands like mv and cd exist here.
/usr/lib: Home to libraries required by applications. Can be source code, scripts, or compiled objects.

/etc: Home to system-wide configuration files.
/home: Contains the home directories for individual users. Your home directory on our Docker image is /home/student. Your shell sessions always start here.

~: Same as /home/${USERNAME}.

/var: A variable directory that holds files changing continuously during operation; for example, log files for applications can be found here under /var/log.
/tmp: A volatile workspace for temporary files. Treat it as a workspace, as systems are typically configured to periodically clean up (delete files) this workspace.


Our Docker Image
There are a few directories in the home directory /home/student that you should be aware of:

/home/student/.config: We will use this to store configuration files; for example, your Git identity.
/home/student/.ssh: We will use this to store keys for SSH authentication, mainly for GitHub.
/home/student/.local: We will use this to install software not included by default. No need for sudo!

Literate Programming

I believe that the time is ripe for significantly better documentation of programs, and that we can best achieve this by considering programs to be works of literature. Hence, my title: “Literate Programming.”
Let us change our traditional attitude to the construction of programs: Instead of imagining that our main task is to instruct a computer what to do, let us concentrate rather on explaining to human beings what we want a computer to do.
The practitioner of literate programming can be regarded as an essayist, whose main concern is with exposition and excellence of style. Such an author, with thesaurus in hand, chooses the names of variables carefully and explains what each variable means. He or she strives for a program that is comprehensible because its concepts have been introduced in an order that is best for human understanding, using a mixture of formal and informal methods that reinforce each other.
